title: Post-exercise hot water immersion induces heat acclimation and improves endurance exercise performance in the heat
authors: Zurawlew MJ, Walsh NP, Fortes MB, Potter C
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: 17 non-heat-acclimatised healthy men (10 in hot water, 7 in thermoneutral water)
findings: Six consecutive days of a 40 min treadmill run at 65% VO2max in temperate conditions (18 C), each followed at once by 40 min of immersion in 40 C water, produced heat acclimation: resting rectal temperature fell 0.27 C and final rectal temperature during submaximal exercise fell 0.28 C at 18 C and 0.36 C at 33 C.
Skin temperature, rectal temperature at sweating onset and RPE were lower in 18 C and 33 C after the six days; physiological strain and thermal sensation were lower at 33 C.

A 5 km treadmill time trial in 33 C improved 4.9% after the hot water days and did not change at 18 C; the control group (34 C water, thermoneutral) showed no change in thermoregulatory measures or performance.
The authors call hot water immersion after exercise a simple, practical and effective heat acclimation strategy.
limitations: Seventeen young men in a laboratory, with a small control group; one six-day protocol, so the effect of fewer days, cooler water or a shorter soak is not tested; the run was 40 min at 65% VO2max, not an easy run for a recreational runner; the performance test was a 5 km treadmill time trial, not a long race; women, older runners and people with health conditions were not studied. Abstract read on Europe PMC; the full text was not read.
implications: Supports counting a day on which a hot bath follows a run of about 40 min as a heat day, as an option and not as a requirement: the dose studied was 40 min at about 40 C on six consecutive days straight after the run.
Gives a dose to state in plain words (soak straight after the run, around 40 min at about 40 C), not a target; no study here tests a shorter soak, a cooler bath or a run shorter than 40 min.
Passive heating after a run adds heat stress; the safety lines (drink, start shorter, not alone at first, get out if dizzy or unwell) come from Heathcote 2018, not from this abstract.
